opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the most confusing things about the current moment. You look at the evals and you think, these models are doing incredibly well, they're solving very hard problems. And then you look at the economic impact, and it seems to lag behind dramatically. That's very difficult to make sense of.

Here's one example. You're using a model for coding. You hit a bug, you tell the model to fix it, and it says, "Oh my God, you're so right, I have a bug, let me fix that." And it introduces a second bug. Then you point out the second bug, and it brings back the first one. You can alternate between these two. How is that possible? It's strange.

I have a couple of possible explanations. One is that RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, so in some ways they're less aware of the broader situation.

The other explanation is about how the RL training is done. In pre-training, the question of what data to use was answered for you: you use all of it. With RL, people have to decide what environments to train on. And I think people, perhaps without fully realizing it, take inspiration from the evals. They say, "I want the model to do really well when we release it, so what RL training would help on this task?" If you combine that with models whose generalization is inadequate, it could explain much of the disconnect between eval performance and what we see in the real world.

A human analogy: imagine two students. One decides to become the best competitive programmer and practices ten thousand hours, memorizes every proof technique, and becomes excellent. The second practices for a hundred hours and also does well. Which one will have the better career? Probably the second. The models are much more like the first student, and even more extreme. They're superbly trained on a narrow distribution, and that doesn't necessarily transfer. The second student has something else, a kind of "it" factor, and I think that's related to the deeper question of generalization, which these models still lack compared to people.

r001.rationale: It says RL can make models too single-minded and narrowly focused, leaving them less aware of the broader situation, and illustrates this with a model repeatedly breaking a coding fix.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pretraining, which uses all available data, with RL, where people must choose training environments.

r003.rationale: It suggests developers may take inspiration from evaluations when choosing RL training environments, perhaps without realizing it.

r004.rationale: It says evaluation-inspired RL combined with inadequate generalization could explain much of the gap between evaluation performance and real-world results.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a very interesting question, and I think it's one of the most important things to understand about where we are right now. So let me try to explain how I think about it.

The models are extremely good at the evals. Like, really extremely good. And then you try to use them for some real task, and they're useful, but they're clearly not as good as the evals would suggest. And there is a gap. So what is going on?

I think there are a few things, and they're all related. The first one is that the evals, in some sense, have become the thing that the labs are optimizing for. Not in a dishonest way. But when you have a lot of very smart people whose job is to make the number go up, and they have a lot of compute, and they have a lot of freedom in how they generate the data, then they will find a way to make the number go up. And the way you make the number go up is you produce a lot of training data that looks like the eval. And so the model gets very good at that distribution. But the real world is not that distribution. The real world is much wider, much messier, much more varied.

So the question is, why does the model generalize so well on the eval and not so well off of it? And I think this is where the deeper issue is, which is that the way these models learn is still quite different from the way people learn. If you take a person, a student, and they study some subject for a reasonable amount of time, they will develop some kind of understanding which transfers. They will be able to handle situations they haven't seen. Whereas the model, you kind of have to show it a lot, a lot of examples of everything. And then it's very good at the things it saw and surprisingly weak at the things it didn't. So I would say the generalization of the models is much worse than the generalization of people, and the evals mask this, because the evals are, by construction, close to things the model has seen.

There is one more thing I'd say. Real-world performance is not just about solving a problem once. It's about doing a long task where you make a mistake and you notice the mistake and you fix it. And this is something the models are still bad at. They don't really learn on the job. A person who is slightly weaker on a test but learns from experience will, after a few months, be much more useful than the model, because the person keeps getting better at the specific thing they're doing, and the model doesn't. So part of the gap is this absence of continual learning. The model is frozen.

So if you put it together, I would say the evals are measuring something real, but they are measuring a narrower thing than people assume. And closing the gap is not going to come from more of the same. It's going to come from models that generalize more like humans, that learn from fewer examples, and that learn while they are being used. That's, I think, the real frontier. And I think we are at the stage where it's back to being a research problem, which is actually exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses narrow evaluation-like training data and weak generalization, but does not mention reinforcement learning or impaired basic-task performance.

r002.rationale: It does not compare reinforcement learning’s choice of training environments with pretraining on all available data.

r003.rationale: It says labs optimize for evaluations by producing similar training data, but does not describe developers using evaluations to design reinforcement learning environments.

r004.rationale: The response links evaluation-like training and poor generalization to the performance gap, but does not identify reinforcement learning as part of that explanation.

astra-6.text:
I think the disconnect tells us something about generalization. A model can be very good at solving a problem when the problem is clearly specified, when all the relevant information is right there, and when there is a relatively clear criterion for success. But in the real world, figuring out what the problem is can be a substantial part of the work.

And there is also a question of reliability. Suppose a model is successful on most individual tasks. That can look very impressive on an evaluation. But if you need it to carry out a long sequence of actions, and a mistake at any point can derail the whole thing, then being successful most of the time is not enough. It needs to recognize its mistakes and recover.

So I don’t think the evaluation results are meaningless. The capabilities are there. But the evaluations measure particular aspects of capability, and it’s tempting to interpret them as measuring something broader. The interesting question is: how much experience does a model need to apply what it knows in a different setting? That is where you start to see the gap between solving a test and doing useful work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization and reliability, but does not mention reinforcement learning or propose that it makes models too narrowly focused.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish how reinforcement learning selects training environments from pretraining’s use of available data.

r003.rationale: It does not say that developers draw inspiration from evaluations when designing reinforcement-learning environments.

r004.rationale: The response links evaluation results to limited generalization, but does not propose the required explanation involving evaluation-inspired reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the evaluations measure something real, but they measure a fairly narrow thing. A model can be very good at answering a well-specified question, where all the relevant information is right there, and still have difficulty doing something useful over a long period of time.

In the real world, you have to figure out what the problem is. You have to notice when you’ve made a mistake, recover from it, and sometimes question the assumptions behind what you’re doing. If you’re good at each individual step but occasionally make an error that you don’t catch, those errors accumulate.

There’s also the question of how much the evaluations resemble what the model has been trained to do. If you put a lot of effort into improving performance on a particular kind of problem, you should expect improvement on that kind of problem. What’s less clear is how broadly that improvement transfers.

So I don’t think the evaluation results are meaningless. I think the gap tells us something about generalization. The models have remarkable capabilities, but those capabilities aren’t yet equally reliable across all the situations in which we’d like to use them.

r002.rationale: It does not compare reinforcement learning’s choice of training environments with pretraining on available data.

r003.rationale: It says improvement on a particular kind of problem may not transfer broadly, but does not say developers use evaluations to shape reinforcement-learning environments.

r004.rationale: The response connects the gap to generalization, but does not attribute it to evaluation-inspired reinforcement learning combined with inadequate generalization.
